messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Lukas had been deployed with a British-led unit when the incident happened, and what still returned to him most sharply was not a single clean image but the broken sequence around it: the helicopter chop overhead, a convoy halt, and the sudden sight of a man on the roadside with his leg split open and blood soaking through his trousers. He had seen injuries before, but that day the sound of aircraft above the dust, the sight of exposed wounds, and the feeling of being trapped while riding with others in a vehicle all seemed to fuse into one unbearable moment. Ever since, he found that he could be standing in his apartment in Brooklyn or at his desk drafting content calendars for his social media clients and, without warning, feel the full force of that day rush back through him with no clear picture attached to it, just a wave of dread and nausea that made him feel as if it were happening again. Other times the memory came in disconnected pieces — the smell of hot metal, a shout, the flash of red — and because it seemed so extreme, Lukas often had the unsettling sense that it could not possibly have happened to him, that it was too unreal, too severe to belong to his life. That strangeness fed his conviction that he had been changed in some permanent way, and with it came the thought that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, that he had failed some basic test of steadiness when others would have held it together.

In the months that followed, Lukas started arranging his life around what might set him off. If he saw visible injuries on someone — a scraped cyclist on the sidewalk, a cut hand in a restaurant, a swollen bruise on his girlfriend’s arm after bumping into a table — he felt his chest lock and immediately began mentally rehearsing what he might say before he had to speak, especially if an interaction was expected. He avoided military and police uniforms in public, and even a glimpse of a weapon in a film or news clip could make him pull away. Driving with other people became difficult because the passenger seat felt too close to being trapped again; he preferred to be alone in the car, if he drove at all. At work, where he often had to move quickly between meetings and screen calls, he became careful to avoid anything that put his body under stress — he skipped the gym, avoided running for the subway, and made excuses when colleagues suggested fast-paced team events. What frightened him most was how quickly his body reacted before he had time to reason with it: a helicopter passing over his neighborhood made his stomach drop and his hands go cold, and the old alarm could be triggered as easily by someone touching his shoulder from behind on the street. Those moments of threat made him more vigilant at night, lying awake because he needed to stay alert, as if sleep itself might let something dangerous creep up on him.

The more Lukas tried to manage these reactions, the more his world narrowed. He began to go over conversations in his head before answering texts, planning sentences in advance even with his girlfriend, and he noticed that this constant checking seemed to keep the event alive rather than contain it. The effort to stay controlled also left him more on edge, and when he was already tense, the same sights and sounds that had become dangerous in his mind — helicopters, injuries, uniforms, being in a car with other people — felt even harder to tolerate. At night, after rehearsing the next day’s interactions and avoiding anything physically taxing, he would still lie awake scanning for sounds outside, and in that exhausted state the fragmented memories came back more easily, usually not as a story but as emotion without image: a pulse of panic, shame, and helplessness that seemed to rise from nowhere. Afterwards he would tell himself, with renewed bitterness, that he was permanently an outsider now, someone who no longer fit in the ordinary world of people who could watch a war scene on television or walk past an ambulance without thinking. He came to believe that his avoidance had not protected him so much as made him more fragile and more different, and that he had somehow made the whole thing harder to bear by trying to control it. In turn, that sense of being damaged and apart made the triggers feel even more charged; every helicopter, every wound, every unexpected touch seemed to confirm that he was no longer the man he had been.

By the time he sought help, Lukas had been living with this tightened circle for months. He had started turning down rides with friends, crossing the street to avoid uniforms, and stepping out of meetings to steady himself after a glimpse of someone injured in a training video. His girlfriend had begun to notice how often he scanned rooms and how often he went quiet when startled. What finally brought him to treatment was that he could no longer ignore how little sleep he was getting and how frightened he felt of his own reactions — of jerking away when touched, of feeling the rush of that day return without warning, of becoming even more cut off from others. He said he was hoping to stop feeling permanently altered, but what scared him most was the possibility that the sense of being an outsider was not a passing state at all, and that this was simply who he had become.
